current: The prohibition on eating fat or blood is stated with unusual force: 'throughout your generations, in all your dwelling places, you shall eat neither fat nor blood' — establishing these as permanent rules, not wilderness-specific practices.
problem: The quoted verse is Leviticus 3:17, in Vayikra, not Tzav. Tzav's own verses (7:23-27) forbid the fat of ox, sheep or goat and blood of bird or animal 'in any of your settlements'.
evidence: Leviticus 3:17 'It is a law for all time throughout the ages, in all your settlements: you must not eat any fat or any blood.' Leviticus 7:23 'You shall eat no fat of ox or sheep or goat'; 7:26 'you must not consume any blood, either of bird or of animal, in any of your settlements.' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Leviticus.7.23-27?version=english
fix: The ban on eating fat and blood is repeated: no fat of ox, sheep or goat, and no blood of bird or animal 'in any of your settlements' (7:23–27), so it applies wherever Israelites live.

current: The blood applied to the right ear, right thumb, and right big toe of the priests during ordination is the same three-point anointing used in the purification ritual for a person healed of tzara'at (a skin affliction) in the next book — suggesting the priests' bodies themselves undergo a kind of purification at ordination.
problem: The tzara'at purification is in Leviticus 14 (parashat Metzora), the same book, not 'the next book'. The conclusion about the priests' bodies being purified is an interpretation stated as the text's meaning.
evidence: Leviticus 14:14 'the priest shall put it on the ridge of the right ear of the one who is being purified, and on the thumb of the right hand, and on the big toe of the right foot.' Leviticus 8:23 same three points for Aaron. https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Leviticus.14.14?version=english
fix: The blood put on the right ear, right thumb and right big toe of the priests at their ordination (8:23–24) is put on the same three places on a person healed of tzara'at, a skin affliction, later in this book (14:14).

current: The requirement that the High Priest bring his own personal grain offering each morning and each evening — and that it must be entirely burned, not eaten — was the subject of debate: Maimonides explains it ensures the High Priest never personally benefits from the offerings he oversees, preventing corruption.
problem: Maimonides gives a different reason: if the priest brought his own small offering and also ate it, it would look as if no service had been done. Nothing about corruption, and no 'debate' is sourced.
evidence: Guide for the Perplexed 3:46: 'The oblation of the priest was entirely burnt (Lev. 6:16), because the priest offered up his oblation by himself, and if he were to offer it, and at the same time to eat it, it would appear as if he had not performed any service.' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Guide_for_the_Perplexed,_Part_3.46
fix: The anointed priest's own grain offering, half in the morning and half in the evening, is burned whole and not eaten (6:13–16). Maimonides (Guide 3:46) explains that if a priest offered his own grain offering and then ate it, it would look as if no service had been done.

current: The prohibition on blood — 'you shall eat no blood in any of your dwelling places' — is so fundamental that it generated one of Judaism's most elaborate practical laws: the salting and washing process (melichah) used to remove blood from meat before cooking, and the separation of meat and milk are both derived from concerns touched on in this and surrounding portions.
problem: The separation of meat and milk is not derived from the blood ban or from these portions; it comes from 'You shall not boil a kid in its mother's milk' (Exodus 23:19, 34:26; Deuteronomy 14:21).
evidence: Exodus 23:19 'You shall not boil a kid in its mother's milk.' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Exodus.23.19?version=english
fix: The ban on blood, 'you must not consume any blood… in any of your settlements' (7:26), is the basis of the Jewish practice of salting and rinsing meat (melichah) to draw out the blood before cooking.

current: The Talmud explains that blood was prohibited because 'the soul of flesh is in the blood' — eating blood would be consuming the animating life-force of another creature, a spiritual category violation. Blood's association with the life-force made it the substance of covenant-making and purification, not ordinary consumption.
problem: The reason 'the life of the flesh is in the blood' is given by the Torah itself (Leviticus 17:11, 14), not the Talmud. 'Spiritual category violation' and the covenant-making generalization are unsourced glosses.
evidence: Leviticus 17:11 'For the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have assigned it to you for making expiation for your lives upon the altar'; 17:14 'You shall not partake of the blood of any flesh, for the life of all flesh is its blood.' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Leviticus.17.11?version=english
fix: The Torah itself gives the reason later in Leviticus: 'the life of the flesh is in the blood,' and blood is set aside for the altar to make atonement (17:11, 14).

current: The seven-day ordination period mirrors preparation periods for priests and temples across the ancient Near East. Mesopotamian texts describe seven-day purification rituals before priests could enter the inner sanctuary.
problem: No source found for Mesopotamian seven-day purifications before entering an inner sanctuary; 'across the ancient Near East' is an unsourced generalization. The standard comparison is the installation of a high priestess at Emar in Syria (Emar 369, c. 1250 BCE).
evidence: Klingbeil, 'The Anointing of Aaron: A Study of Leviticus 8:12', AUSS: 'Emar 369 provides an early ANE instance of anointing a priest' https://digitalcommons.andrews.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2597&context=auss ; Sapiru Project translation of Emar 369: 'For seven days, on each day, at the NIN.DINGIR's house, they offer two sheep to the gods' (text c. 1250 BCE, Emar, Syria) https://sapiru.wordpress.com/2024/03/24/enthronement-of-baals-high-priestess/
fix: A text from Emar in Syria from about 1250 BCE (Emar 369) describes the installation of a high priestess over several days, with anointing and sacrifices, including seven days of daily offerings; scholars compare it with the ordination in Leviticus 8.

current: The application of blood to extremities of the body (ear for hearing divine commands, thumb for skilled action, big toe for walking in holy paths) is an ancient ritual logic of consecration: the officiant is being marked as wholly dedicated, from the faculty of hearing to the capacity for action to the means of movement.
problem: This is one later symbolic reading stated as the ancient meaning. The text gives no reason, and the same rite is used to purify a healed person (14:14), which does not fit a consecration-only reading.
evidence: Leviticus 8:23-24 (blood on right ear, thumb, big toe) and 14:14 (same rite for 'the one who is being purified'); the verses state no symbolism. https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Leviticus.8.23-24?version=english
fix: The Torah does not explain why blood is put on the right ear, thumb and big toe. Later readers have seen in it hearing, doing and walking, but that is interpretation; the same rite is used for a person healed of tzara'at (14:14).

current: The Ordination of Aaron and his Sons — Julius Schnorr von Carolsfeld, 1860
problem: The file is an 1890 Holman Bible illustration of the Tabernacle's altar of incense, altar of burnt offering and laver, not a Schnorr von Carolsfeld ordination scene. It is an artwork of objects, not the ordination.
evidence: Commons File:Holman Altar of Incense Altar of Burnt-Offering Laver.jpg: description 'The Altar of Incense, Altar of Burnt-Offering, and Laver from the Biblical Tabernacle; illustration from the 1890 Holman Bible'; Artist 'illustrators of the 1890 Holman Bible'; date 1890. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Holman_Altar_of_Incense_Altar_of_Burnt-Offering_Laver.jpg
fix: The Altar of Incense, Altar of Burnt Offering and Laver — Holman Bible illustrators, 1890

current: On the eighth day of the ordination, Aaron and his sons offer their first sacrifices and God's fire consumes the altar in a divine sign. Then Aaron's sons Nadav and Abihu offer "strange fire" that God had not commanded, and are struck dead. God commands Aaron not to publicly mourn.
problem: The fire consumes the burnt offering and the fat on the altar, not the altar. It is Moses, not God, who tells Aaron and his sons not to bare their heads or rend their clothes.
evidence: Leviticus 9:24 'Fire came forth from before GOD and consumed the burnt offering and the fat parts on the altar.' Leviticus 10:6 'And Moses said to Aaron and to his sons Eleazar and Ithamar, "Do not bare your heads and do not rend your clothes, lest you die…"' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Leviticus.10.2-7?version=english
fix: On the eighth day of the ordination, Aaron and his sons offer their first sacrifices, and fire from God consumes the burnt offering on the altar. Then Aaron's sons Nadav and Abihu offer "strange fire" that God had not commanded, and are struck dead. Moses tells Aaron and his surviving sons not to show the signs of mourning.

current: They die in front of the altar.
problem: The text says they died 'before GOD' (lifnei YHWH), and their bodies are carried 'from the front of the sanctuary'; it does not say in front of the altar.
evidence: Leviticus 10:2 'thus they died by GOD's will (Lit. "before GOD")'; 10:4 'carry your kinsmen away from the front of the sanctuary'. https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Leviticus.10.2-7?version=english
fix: They die 'before God', and their cousins carry them out from the front of the sanctuary (10:2–5).

current: Moses then instructs Aaron and his surviving sons to continue the service without removing their priestly garments or publicly mourning — lest the people interpret grief as a sign that the divine service itself is in question.
problem: The reason given is invented. The Torah's reason is 'lest you die and anger strike the whole community', and 'do not go outside the entrance of the Tent of Meeting… for GOD's anointing oil is upon you'; the rest of Israel is told to mourn.
evidence: Leviticus 10:6-7 'Do not bare your heads and do not rend your clothes, lest you die and anger strike the whole community. But your kin, all the house of Israel, shall bewail the burning… do not go outside the entrance of the Tent of Meeting, lest you die, for GOD's anointing oil is upon you.' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Leviticus.10.2-7?version=english
fix: Moses tells Aaron and his surviving sons not to bare their heads or tear their clothes, 'lest you die and anger strike the whole community', and not to leave the Tent of Meeting, because the anointing oil is on them; the rest of Israel is to mourn the dead (10:6–7).

current: The Talmud (Eruvin 63a) gives all of these explanations without choosing one, suggesting the mystery is intentional.
problem: Eruvin 63a gives only one explanation (Rabbi Eliezer: they ruled on a point of law in front of Moses). The list of explanations is collected in Vayikra Rabbah 20. 'Suggesting the mystery is intentional' is unsourced.
evidence: Eruvin 63a: 'Rabbi Eliezer says: The sons of Aaron died only because they issued a halakhic ruling before Moses, their teacher' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Eruvin.63a ; Vayikra Rabbah 20:8 'Due to four matters Aaron's sons died: For drawing near; for sacrificing; for alien fire; and because they did not take counsel from one another'; 20:9 'Because they were intoxicated with wine'; 20:10 'Rabbi Levi said: They were arrogant.' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Vayikra_Rabbah.20.9
fix: The midrash Vayikra Rabbah (chapter 20) collects many of these explanations side by side; the Talmud (Eruvin 63a) records Rabbi Eliezer's view that they died for deciding a point of law in front of Moses.

current: The silence of Aaron ('vayidom Aharon') in response to the death of his sons is one of the Torah's most powerful moments, cited by the rabbis as the highest form of acceptance of divine judgment — and as the source of the tradition of silent mourning in the presence of grief.
problem: No source found calling it 'the highest form of acceptance' or making it the source of silent mourning. The Talmud derives that comforters stay silent until the mourner speaks from Job (Moed Katan 28b). What Rashi and the Talmud do say is that Aaron was rewarded for his silence.
evidence: Rashi on Leviticus 10:3: 'AND AARON WAS SILENT — He received a reward for his silence… the subsequent Divine address was made to him alone' (Zevachim 115b) https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Rashi_on_Leviticus.10.3 ; Moed Katan 28b: 'The consolers are not permitted to speak words of consolation until the mourner opens and speaks first. As it is stated: "…none spoke a word to him… After this Job opened his mouth"' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Moed_Katan.28b
fix: Aaron's silence ('vayidom Aharon', 10:3) is one of the Torah's most remembered moments. Rashi, following the Talmud (Zevachim 115b), says Aaron was rewarded for his silence: the next command, about priests and wine (10:8–11), was spoken to him alone.

current: The full halakhic system — prohibiting mixing meat and milk, requiring separate dishes, salting meat to remove blood, buying from supervised slaughterhouses — developed gradually over the Talmudic and medieval periods as extensions of the biblical foundations here.
problem: Meat-and-milk rules (and separate dishes) do not extend this portion; they rest on 'do not boil a kid in its mother's milk' (Exodus 23:19 and parallels). Salting relates to the blood ban (Leviticus 7:26, 17:10-14), not Shemini.
evidence: Exodus 23:19 'You shall not boil a kid in its mother's milk.' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Exodus.23.19?version=english ; Leviticus 11 contains only the permitted/forbidden species and impurity of carcasses.
fix: The fuller system of kashrut, including the rules on meat and milk (from Exodus 23:19) and salting meat to remove blood, developed over the Talmudic and medieval periods, building on these and other biblical laws.

current: The laws function primarily as markers of communal identity and dietary discipline.
problem: A scholarly theory stated as settled fact. The only reason Leviticus itself gives is holiness.
evidence: Leviticus 11:44-45 'you shall sanctify yourselves and be holy, for I am holy… you shall be holy, for I am holy.' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Leviticus.11.44-45?version=english
fix: Many scholars see the laws as marking Israel off from its neighbors; Leviticus itself gives holiness as the reason: 'you shall be holy, for I am holy' (11:44–45).

current: The Death of Nadab and Abihu — Gustave Doré, 1866
problem: The file is James Tissot's (or a follower's) 'Moses and Joshua in the Tabernacle', c. 1896–1902, Jewish Museum New York. It is not by Doré and shows a different scene (Exodus 33:11), not Nadab and Abihu. Commons has Tissot's 'The Two Priests Are Destroyed' (Leviticus 10:2) as a correct-scene replacement.
evidence: Commons File:Tissot Moses and Joshua in the Tabernacle.jpg: 'Moses and Joshua in the Tabernacle, c. 1896-1902, by James Jacques Joseph Tissot (French, 1836-1902) or follower… at the Jewish Museum, New York' https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Tissot_Moses_and_Joshua_in_the_Tabernacle.jpg ; File:Tissot The Two Priests Are Destroyed.jpg: 'Nadab and Abihu are killed in the Tabernacle, Leviticus 10:2', James Tissot, between 1896 and 1900 https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Tissot_The_Two_Priests_Are_Destroyed.jpg
fix: If the image is kept: "Moses and Joshua in the Tabernacle — James Tissot or follower, c. 1896–1902" (wrong scene; better replace). If replaced with File:Tissot_The_Two_Priests_Are_Destroyed.jpg: "The Two Priests Are Destroyed — James Tissot, c. 1896–1900"

current: ...at the end of which she brings a lamb (or two birds if she cannot afford a lamb) as a burnt and sin offering.
problem: The lamb is only the burnt offering; the sin (purgation) offering is a pigeon or turtledove. Only a woman who cannot afford a lamb brings two birds, one for each.
evidence: Leviticus 12:6 'a lamb in its first year for a burnt offering, and a pigeon or a turtledove for a purgation offering'; 12:8 'If… her means do not suffice for a sheep, she shall take two turtledoves or two pigeons, one for a burnt offering and the other for a purgation offering.' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Leviticus.12.6-8?version=english
fix: A woman who gives birth enters a period of ritual impurity, seven days for a son, fourteen for a daughter, followed by a longer period of blood-purification, at the end of which she brings a lamb as a burnt offering and a pigeon or turtledove as a purgation offering; if she cannot afford a lamb, she brings two birds, one for each (12:6–8).

current: a skin affliction that is almost certainly not modern leprosy (which was unknown in the ancient Near East in this form) but rather a range of skin conditions treated as indicators of ritual status.
problem: The claim that leprosy was 'unknown in the ancient Near East in this form' has no source found; the reference consulted says only that tzara'at is not Hansen's disease.
evidence: Wikipedia, 'Tzaraath': 'it is not Hansen's disease, the disease known as "leprosy" in modern times'; no statement on when leprosy reached the Near East. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tzaraath
fix: Then tzara'at occupies the rest of the portion: a skin affliction that scholars do not identify with Hansen's disease (modern leprosy), treated here as a matter of ritual status.

current: The two-tiered offering after childbirth — a lamb for those who could afford it, two birds for those who could not — reflects the Torah's consistent concern for economic accessibility in ritual: no law of purification should be impossible for the poor to fulfill.
problem: The 'two-tiered' description is inaccurate (the better-off mother brings a lamb and a bird), and 'no law of purification should be impossible for the poor' is an unsourced generalization. What the text shows is that the poorer offering appears in several places.
evidence: Leviticus 12:6-8 (lamb plus bird; or two birds); 14:21-22 'If, however, the person is poor… two turtledoves or two pigeons—depending on their means'; 5:7-11 sliding scale. https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Leviticus.14.21-22?version=english
fix: A mother who cannot afford a lamb brings two birds instead (12:8). Leviticus offers the same kind of cheaper option for some purgation offerings (5:7–13) and for a person healed of tzara'at (14:21–32).

current: The laws of lashon hara, elaborated extensively by the 19th-century rabbi Chofetz Chaim (Rabbi Israel Meir Kagan), are one of the most developed areas of Jewish ethical law, all ultimately rooted in the Tazria-Metzora narrative.
problem: The ban on gossip and slander rests mainly on Leviticus 19:16, 'lo telech rachil' (in Kedoshim), not on Tazria-Metzora; the rabbis link tzara'at to lashon hara as a punishment, not as the source of the laws. Rabbi Kagan (1838–1933) also lived well into the 20th century.
evidence: Leviticus 19:16 'Do not deal basely with (others: "go about as a talebearer among") members of your people' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Leviticus.19.16?version=english ; Arakhin 16a lists malicious speech among causes of tzara'at https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Arakhin.16a
fix: The laws of lashon hara were set out in detail by Rabbi Israel Meir Kagan in his book Chofetz Chaim (1873). The main verse behind them is 'do not go about as a talebearer' (19:16); the rabbis' link between tzara'at and evil speech made these portions a common place to teach them.

current: The system of priestly examination, quarantine, re-examination, and declaration of status mirrors infectious disease protocols remarkably well for a pre-germ-theory society, functioning as a community health management system administered through the religious authority.
problem: A public-health reading stated as fact. The text treats tzara'at as impurity, and some rules cut against a contagion logic: a person covered from head to foot is declared pure, and a house is emptied before inspection so its contents are not made impure.
evidence: Leviticus 13:13 'if the priest sees that the eruption has covered the whole body—he shall pronounce as pure the affected person'; 14:36 'The priest shall order the house cleared before the priest enters… so that nothing in the house may become impure.' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Leviticus.13.12-13?version=english
fix: Some readers see a public-health logic in the quarantine, but the text treats tzara'at as ritual impurity: a person covered from head to foot is declared pure (13:12–13), and a house is emptied before the priest looks so that its contents do not become impure (14:36).

current: Moses in the Wilderness — Julius Schnorr von Carolsfeld, 1860
problem: The file is Frederick Goodall's 'The Poor Widow's Offering' (dated only 'before 1904'), a woman holding two doves; the Commons page notes 'as in Leviticus 12:8'. Not Schnorr, not Moses. The scene fits Tazria (a poor mother's bird offering), though the title says widow.
evidence: Commons File:Goodall The Poor Widow's Offering.jpg: description 'The Poor Widow's Offering'; Artist 'Frederick Goodall'; date 'before 1904'; notes 'as in Leviticus 12:8'. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Goodall_The_Poor_Widow%27s_Offering.jpg
fix: The Poor Widow's Offering — Frederick Goodall

current: The portion closes with laws of ritual impurity from bodily discharges — for men (seminal emissions) and women (menstrual blood), each requiring immersion in a ritual bath (mikveh) for purification.
problem: The Torah tells a man to 'bathe his body in water' (fresh water for an abnormal discharge); it does not name a mikveh, and for the menstruant or a woman with a discharge it states no bathing at all (15:19, 28). Immersion for her is rabbinic interpretation. The chapter also covers abnormal discharges for both sexes, not only emissions and menstruation.
evidence: Leviticus 15:13 'wash those clothes, and bathe in fresh water; then he shall be pure'; 15:16 'he shall bathe his whole body in water and remain impure until evening'; 15:19 'she shall remain in her menstrual separation seven days'; 15:28 'she shall count off seven days, and after that she shall be pure.' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Leviticus.15.13?version=english
fix: The portion closes with laws of impurity from bodily discharges, normal and abnormal, for men and for women. A man is told to bathe in water (15:13, 16); for women the text gives a count of days (15:19, 28), and the rabbis read immersion in a ritual bath (mikveh) into these laws as well.

current: The two-bird ritual — one slaughtered, one released — is one of the most evocative symbolic ceremonies in all of Torah, and has no parallel elsewhere in the sacrificial system.
problem: The same two-bird rite is used again in this portion to purify a house (14:49-53), and the Yom Kippur rite of two goats, one slaughtered and one sent away alive, is a close parallel (16:8-10, 21-22).
evidence: Leviticus 14:49-53 'To purge the house, he shall take two birds… He shall slaughter the one bird… he shall set the live bird free outside the city in the open country.' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Leviticus.14.49-53?version=english
fix: In the two-bird rite, one bird is slaughtered and the other, dipped in its blood, is set free (14:4–7). The same rite purifies a house (14:49–53), and the two goats of Yom Kippur, one offered and one sent away, follow a similar pattern (16:8–10).

current: House tzara'at — a supernatural affliction striking the actual walls of a building — is considered so rare that the Talmud (Negaim 12:5) says it never actually occurred and was written 'only to study and receive reward,' a legal category that exists purely theoretically.
problem: Mishnah Negaim 12:5 describes how a priest inspects a house; it says nothing of the kind. The 'never was and never will be' teaching is an anonymous baraita in Sanhedrin 71a, and the same page records two rabbis who say they saw places where plagued houses had stood. So it is one view, not the Talmud's settled position.
evidence: Mishnah Negaim 12:5: 'What is the procedure for the inspection of a house?…' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Mishnah_Negaim.12.5 ; Sanhedrin 71a: 'There has never been a house afflicted with leprosy of the house and there will never be one in the future. And why, then, was the passage… written…? So that you may expound… and receive reward'; 'Rabbi Eliezer, son of Rabbi Tzadok, says: There was a place in the area of Gaza, and it was called the leprous ruin'; 'Rabbi Shimon of the village of Akko said: …stones afflicted with leprosy were cast there.' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Sanhedrin.71a
fix: One teaching in the Talmud (Sanhedrin 71a) says a house with tzara'at never existed and the law was written only to be studied for reward; on the same page, two rabbis say they saw places where such houses had stood, near Gaza and in the Galilee.

current: The continuity of the mikveh from the wilderness laws to 21st-century Jewish life is one of the longest unbroken institutional threads in religious history.
problem: Traditional chronology stated as history plus an unsourced superlative. Archaeologically, mikvaot first appear in the first century BCE.
evidence: Wikipedia, 'Mikveh': 'Mikvot first appear in the historical record in that century [first century BCE], and from that time, ancient mikvot are found across the Land of Israel.' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mikveh
fix: Stepped immersion pools appear in the archaeological record by the first century BCE, and Jews have kept using the mikveh ever since.

current: Archaeologists have discovered mikvaot at almost every excavated Jewish site from the Second Temple period onward: at Masada, Qumran, Jericho, and in hundreds of private homes in Jerusalem.
problem: 'Almost every excavated Jewish site' and 'hundreds of private homes in Jerusalem' are not supported by the source found; it says hundreds across the Land of Israel.
evidence: Wikipedia, 'Mikveh': 'Hundreds of mikvot from the Second Temple period have been discovered so far across the Land of Israel'; sites named include Qumran, Masada, Jerusalem. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mikveh
fix: Archaeologists have found hundreds of mikvaot from the Second Temple period across the Land of Israel, including at Masada, Qumran and Jerusalem.

current: The requirement for naturally gathered water ('living water' — spring or rainwater) rather than drawn water is specified here and defines mikveh architecture to this day.
problem: 'Living' (fresh) water in 15:13 means spring or running water, not rainwater, and the ban on drawn water is rabbinic, not specified in the Torah. The verse usually cited for the gathered pool is 11:36 (in Shemini).
evidence: Leviticus 15:13 'bathe in fresh water'; 11:36 'a spring or cistern in which water is collected shall be pure' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Leviticus.11.36?version=english ; Wikipedia, 'Mikveh': 'the prohibition on using pumped water for a mikveh is rabbinic, not biblical' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mikveh
fix: The Torah speaks of 'a spring or cistern in which water is collected' (11:36) and of bathing in fresh, flowing water (15:13); the rabbis added the rule against drawn water that still shapes how a mikveh is built.

current: https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b0/032.The_Plague_of_Leprosy_%28Miriam%29.jpg/330px-... ; The Plague of Leprosy (Miriam) — Gustave Doré, 1866
problem: The file does not exist on Commons: the thumbnail URL returns HTTP 404 and the Commons API reports the page as missing, so the image is broken. Even if it existed, Miriam's affliction is in Numbers 12, not Metzora; and on Commons the Doré plate numbered 031 is 'The Finding of Moses', so 032 would not be a Numbers scene.
evidence: curl -I thumbnail URL → 'HTTP/2 404'; Commons API query for File:032.The Plague of Leprosy (Miriam).jpg → "missing". Commons search shows 'File:031.The Finding of Moses.jpg'.
fix: Replace the image with a real Commons file showing Leviticus 14 (for example a leper's purification scene), and caption it from its Commons page in the form 'Title — Artist, Year'. Until then remove doreImageUrl/doreImageCaption.

current: Two identical goats are brought; lots are cast over them: one for YHWH (sacrificed), one for Azazel (the scapegoat).
problem: The Torah says only 'two he-goats'. That they must be alike is a rabbinic rule (Mishnah Yoma 6:1), stated here as the text.
evidence: Leviticus 16:5 'he shall take two he-goats for a purgation offering and a ram for a burnt offering.' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Leviticus.16.5?version=english
fix: Two he-goats are brought, and lots are cast over them: one for YHWH (sacrificed), one for Azazel (the scapegoat).

current: The day itself is characterized by complete fasting ('afflicting the soul') and rest — even the foreigner living among Israel must observe it.
problem: The text commands 'self-denial', which the rabbis define as fasting and other abstentions; the resident alien is named in connection with 'you shall do no manner of work', not the self-denial.
evidence: Leviticus 16:29 'you shall practice self-denial; and you shall do no manner of work, neither the citizen nor the alien who resides among you.' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Leviticus.16.29?version=english ; Mishnah Yoma 8:1 lists eating, drinking, bathing, anointing, shoes, relations https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Mishnah_Yoma.8.1
fix: The day is one of self-denial, which the rabbis define as fasting and other abstentions, and of rest from all work, for the citizen and for the resident alien (16:29).

current: In Second Temple times, the goat was led to a cliff called Beit Hadudo twelve miles east of Jerusalem and pushed off; a thread of crimson wool tied to its horns was said to turn white if the atonement was accepted — a custom mentioned in the Talmud (Yoma 67b) as no longer working in the forty years before the Temple's destruction.
problem: The Mishnah puts the cliff 12 mil (a mil is about 1 km, not a mile) from Jerusalem, with no direction; Rabbi Yehuda names Beit Hiddudo as three mil away, so the name and the 12-mil distance are not one claim. Half the thread was tied to the rock and half between the horns. The forty-years statement is in Yoma 39b, not 67b.
evidence: Mishnah Yoma 6:4 'ten booths from Jerusalem to the cliff… the total distance was twelve mil'; 6:6 'half of the strip tied to the rock, and half of it tied between the two horns of the goat. And he pushed the goat backward'; 6:8 'Rabbi Yehuda said… From Jerusalem to Beit Ḥiddudo… was a distance of three mil' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Mishnah_Yoma.6.4 ; Yoma 39b 'during the forty years prior to the destruction of the Second Temple… the strip of crimson wool that was tied to the head of the goat that was sent to Azazel did not turn white' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Yoma.39b
fix: According to the Mishnah (Yoma 6:4–6), in Second Temple times the goat was led to a cliff twelve mil (roughly 12 km) from Jerusalem and pushed off, with a crimson thread tied half to a rock and half between its horns. The Talmud (Yoma 39b) says the thread was said to turn white when atonement was granted, but did not in the forty years before the Temple was destroyed.

current: ...a full twenty-five-hour fast, extensive prayer in synagogue, and abstention from five 'afflictions' (food, drink, bathing, anointing, leather shoes, and marital relations).
problem: Says five and then lists six. The count of five treats eating and drinking as one.
evidence: Mishnah Yoma 8:1 'it is prohibited to engage in eating and in drinking, and in bathing, and in smearing oil on one's body, and in wearing shoes, and in conjugal relations.' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Mishnah_Yoma.8.1
fix: ...a fast of about twenty-five hours, long prayers in synagogue, and five abstentions: eating and drinking, bathing, anointing with oil, wearing leather shoes, and marital relations (Mishnah Yoma 8:1).

current: The white kittel (robe) worn by the prayer leader and many worshippers on Yom Kippur mirrors the white linen garments the High Priest wore when entering the Holy of Holies.
problem: This is one popular explanation stated as fact. The Rema, the standard source for the custom, gives two other reasons: white like the ministering angels, and the kittel is like a burial shroud, which humbles the heart.
evidence: Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 610:4 (Rema): 'it is customary to dress in clean, white clothes on Yom Kippur, analogous to the ministering angels, and likewise it is customary to wear a kittel which is white and clean, and it is also the clothing of the dead (the shroud), and therefore the heart of a man is humbled and broken' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Shulchan_Arukh,_Orach_Chayim.610
fix: Many worshippers wear a white kittel on Yom Kippur. The Rema (Orach Chayim 610:4) explains it as dressing in white like the angels and as a reminder of the burial shroud; some also connect it with the High Priest's white linen.

current: Hittite 'scapegoat' rituals sent a donkey laden with offerings into enemy territory to carry evil away.
problem: No source found for a Hittite donkey rite. The standard Hittite parallel (the ritual of Ashella, 13th century BCE) sends a ram with a decorated head toward the enemy's land to end a plague.
evidence: TheTorah.com, 'Scapegoat: The Origins of the Crimson Thread': the prescription of Ashella (13th century BCE): army commanders each prepare a ram and 'lead the ram to the road leading to the enemy's land', 'the ram with decorated head' to make peace with the god causing the plague. https://www.thetorah.com/article/scapegoat-the-origins-of-the-crimson-thread
fix: A Hittite ritual of the 13th century BCE, the ritual of Ashella, sends rams with decorated heads toward the enemy's land to take a plague away from the army.

current: The High Priest Enters the Sanctuary — Julius Schnorr von Carolsfeld, 1860
problem: The file is William Holman Hunt's painting 'The Scapegoat', 1854. The scene is right for the portion; the title and artist are wrong.
evidence: Commons File:The Scapegoat.jpg: title 'The Scapegoat'; Artist 'William Holman Hunt'; date 1854. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:The_Scapegoat.jpg
fix: The Scapegoat — William Holman Hunt, 1854

current: ...honor your parents, keep the Sabbath...
problem: Leviticus 19:3 commands revering (tira'u, 'fear') mother and father; 'honor' is the Ten Commandments' wording (Exodus 20:12). The narrative on the same page correctly says 'fear'.
evidence: Leviticus 19:3 'You shall each revere your mother and your father, and keep My sabbaths.' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Leviticus.19.3?version=english
fix: The Holiness Code calls on Israel to be holy as God is holy. A dense collection of ethical and ritual laws follows: revere your mother and father, keep the Sabbath, leave the corners of your field for the poor, do not steal or lie, do not hate your brother, love your neighbor as yourself. Prohibitions against pagan practices and penalties for violations are included.

current: Don't cross-breed animals, mix crops, or weave linen and wool together.
problem: Leviticus 19:19 forbids cloth 'from a mixture of two kinds of material' without naming them; wool and linen are named in Deuteronomy 22:11.
evidence: Leviticus 19:19 'you shall not put on cloth from a mixture of two kinds of material'; Deuteronomy 22:11 'You shall not wear cloth combining wool and linen.' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Leviticus.19.19?version=english
fix: Don't cross-breed animals, sow two kinds of seed in a field, or wear cloth of two kinds of material mixed (19:19; Deuteronomy 22:11 names them as wool and linen).

current: Leviticus 19:18 — 'Love your neighbor as yourself' — is arguably the most quoted verse in the entire Hebrew Bible in the Western tradition: Rabbi Akiva called it 'the great principle of the Torah,' Hillel stated the entire Torah was a commentary on it, and it became foundational to Jewish ethical philosophy and to Western moral thought more broadly.
problem: 'Most quoted verse' is an unsourced superlative. Hillel did not say the Torah is a commentary on this verse; he gave his own negative rule ('what is hateful to you…') as the whole Torah, with the rest its interpretation. The link to 19:18 is a later reading (the Targum attributed to Jonathan renders 19:18 in the same negative form).
evidence: Sifra Kedoshim 4:12: 'R. Akiva says: This is an all-embracing principle in the Torah' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Sifra,_Kedoshim,_Chapter_4.12 ; Shabbat 31a (Hillel): 'That which is hateful to you do not do to another; that is the entire Torah, and the rest is its interpretation. Go study.' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Shabbat.31a ; Targum Jonathan on Lev 19:18: 'ותרחמי לחברך דמן אנת סני לך לא תעביד ליה' (love your fellow: what you hate, do not do to him) https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Targum_Jonathan_on_Leviticus.19.18?version=hebrew
fix: Leviticus 19:18, 'Love your neighbor as yourself', is one of the Torah's best-known verses. Rabbi Akiva called it 'a great principle of the Torah' (Sifra). Hillel's famous saying, 'What is hateful to you, do not do to another; that is the entire Torah, and the rest is its interpretation' (Shabbat 31a), is often read as a restatement of it, and the Aramaic Targum attributed to Jonathan renders the verse in just that form.

current: The original Hebrew context specifies 'neighbor' as a fellow Israelite, but immediately following verses extend the same obligation to the 'stranger who dwells among you' (verse 34)
problem: Verse 34 is sixteen verses later, not 'immediately following'.
evidence: Leviticus 19:34 'The strangers who reside with you shall be to you as your citizens; you shall love each one as yourself, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt.' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Leviticus.19.34?version=english
fix: In context 'neighbor' parallels 'members of your people', but later in the same chapter the same words are applied to the stranger: 'you shall love each one as yourself, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt' (19:34).

current: The 'great rule of Torah' (klal gadol ba-Torah) attributed to Hillel — 'what is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbor; the rest is commentary, go and study' — is his reformulation of Leviticus 19:18.
problem: 'Klal gadol ba-Torah' is Rabbi Akiva's phrase about Leviticus 19:18 (Sifra), not Hillel's. Hillel's saying (Shabbat 31a) does not cite 19:18; calling it his reformulation is an interpretation.
evidence: Sifra Kedoshim 4:12: 'R. Akiva says: This is an all-embracing principle (klal gadol) in the Torah' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Sifra,_Kedoshim,_Chapter_4.12 ; Shabbat 31a: 'That which is hateful to you do not do to another; that is the entire Torah, and the rest is its interpretation. Go study.' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Shabbat.31a
fix: Rabbi Akiva called 'love your neighbor as yourself' a great principle of the Torah (klal gadol ba-Torah). Hillel taught, 'What is hateful to you, do not do to another; that is the entire Torah, and the rest is its interpretation. Go study' (Shabbat 31a), a saying often linked to this verse.

current: The prohibition on 'pe'at ha-sadeh' (corners of the field) left for the poor reflects a redistributive agricultural policy well-attested in other ancient Near Eastern societies, where temple institutions often administered poor relief through grain distribution.
problem: No source found for gleaning-type laws being 'well-attested' elsewhere in the ancient Near East; temple rations are a different thing. It is also not a 'prohibition on pe'at ha-sadeh' but a command to leave the edge unharvested.
evidence: Leviticus 19:9-10 'you shall not reap all the way to the edges of your field, or gather the gleanings… you shall leave them for the poor and the stranger.' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Leviticus.19.9-10?version=english
fix: The command to leave the edge of the field (pe'at ha-sadeh), the gleanings and the fallen grapes 'for the poor and the stranger' (19:9–10) puts care for the poor into the farmer's own harvest.

current: Moses Proclaims the Holiness Code — Julius Schnorr von Carolsfeld, 1860
problem: The file is a July 2005 photograph of a wheat field in the Pays de Caux, Normandy, by Commons user Urban, not an artwork and not Schnorr. It can illustrate the field-corner law only as a modern photo.
evidence: Commons File:Wheat field caux.jpg: 'Wheat field (champ de blé), Pays de Caux, Normandy. I took this picture on July 2005. [[User:Urban|Urban]]'; licence GFDL/CC BY-SA 3.0. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Wheat_field_caux.jpg
fix: A wheat field in Normandy (photo) — Urban, Wikimedia Commons, 2005  [photo, not an artwork; CC BY-SA 3.0 needs attribution; consider replacing with an artwork of gleaning, e.g. a Ruth scene, or keep and label as a photo]

current: Physical blemishes — a catalog of twenty physical conditions from blindness to a broken limb to an unusual nose — disqualify a priest from performing the Temple service (though not from eating priestly portions).
problem: Leviticus 21:18-20 lists twelve defects, not twenty.
evidence: Leviticus 21:18-20 'no man who is blind, or lame, or has a limb too short or too long; no man who has a broken leg or a broken arm; or who is a hunchback, or a dwarf, or who has a growth in his eye, or who has a boil-scar, or scurvy, or crushed testes.' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Leviticus.21.18-20?version=english
fix: Physical defects, twelve are listed, from blindness to a broken limb (21:18–20), disqualify a priest from offering at the altar, though not from eating the priests' share (21:22).

current: Passover in the first month with the Omer counting beginning the next day; Shavuot fifty days after the Omer (Pentecost)
problem: The text dates the omer to 'the day after the sabbath', whose meaning was disputed in antiquity (the rabbis read it as the day after the first festival day; the Boethusians as Sunday). The count runs seven weeks, and the new-grain offering comes on the fiftieth day.
evidence: Leviticus 23:15-16 'from the day on which you bring the sheaf of elevation offering—the day after the sabbath—you shall count off seven weeks… until the day after the seventh week—fifty days' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Leviticus.23.15-16?version=english ; Menachot 65a on the Boethusians 'who would say that the festival of Shavuot always occurs after Shabbat, on a Sunday' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Menachot.65a
fix: Passover in the first month, with the counting of the omer beginning 'the day after the sabbath'; after seven weeks, on the fiftieth day, the festival later called Shavuot (Pentecost).

current: Pharisees counted from the day after the first day of Passover; Sadducees from the day after the first Shabbat during Passover — a dispute that led to Shavuot falling on different days, a disagreement that echoes to this day between different communities.
problem: The Talmud names the opposing group as the Boethusians (often grouped with the Sadducees) and says they held that Shavuot always falls on a Sunday. 'Echoes to this day between different communities' names no one and was not verified here (see could-not-check).
evidence: Menachot 65a: 'the Boethusians would say that the festival of Shavuot always occurs after Shabbat, on a Sunday. Their reasoning was that the verse states… "from the morrow after the day of rest [hashabbat]"' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Menachot.65a
fix: The rabbis counted from the day after the first day of Passover; the Boethusians, a group the Talmud opposes, counted from the Sunday after Shabbat, so for them Shavuot always fell on a Sunday (Menachot 65a).

current: Emor contains the Torah's most complete single listing of the mo'adim — the appointed festivals — making it one of the most liturgically significant portions in the calendar.
problem: Numbers 28–29 is also a full list of the fixed times, and it adds the New Moon, which Leviticus 23 lacks; 'most complete' is not accurate.
evidence: Numbers 28:9 'On the sabbath day…'; 28:11 'On your new moons you shall present a burnt offering'; 29:12 'On the fifteenth day of the seventh month…' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Numbers.28.11?version=english
fix: Emor contains one of the Torah's two full lists of the appointed festivals (Leviticus 23); the other, in Numbers 28–29, gives the offerings for each day and adds the New Moon.

current: The word 'mo'ed' (appointed time) is used repeatedly, and the rabbis read it as establishing that God has set specific times for encountering the divine — making the calendar itself a theological statement about when the gap between human and divine narrows.
problem: No rabbinic source found for this reading. The best-known rabbinic reading of these verses is the opposite emphasis: 'which you shall proclaim' teaches that the court's declaration fixes the festival dates, even if it erred.
evidence: Rosh Hashanah 25a: '"you shall proclaim them [otam]"… Three times the verses use the term: Them [otam], which can also be read as you [atem]… You are authorized to determine'; '…whether you have proclaimed them at their proper time or whether you have declared them not at their proper time, I have only these Festivals' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Rosh_Hashanah.25a
fix: The chapter repeats that these are times 'you shall proclaim' (23:2, 4, 37). The Talmud (Rosh Hashanah 25a) reads this to mean that the court's declaration of the new month fixes the festival dates, even if the court was mistaken.

current: ...derived from the 'boughs of goodly trees, branches of palm trees, boughs of leafy trees, and willows of the brook' commanded here.
problem: The Hebrew is 'pri etz hadar', the fruit (product) of hadar trees, which is why it is the citron; 'boughs of goodly trees' is the King James mistranslation.
evidence: Leviticus 23:40 'you shall take the product of hadar trees (Traditionally the product is understood as "citron"), branches of palm trees, boughs of leafy trees, and willows of the brook' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Leviticus.23.40?version=english
fix: The lulav and etrog, palm frond, willow, myrtle and citron, waved on Sukkot are among Judaism's best-known ritual objects, taken from 'the fruit of hadar trees, branches of palm trees, boughs of leafy trees, and willows of the brook' (23:40).

current: These agricultural festivals were common across the ancient Near East — the Ugaritic texts describe very similar seasonal celebrations. The Torah transforms them by attaching historical meaning
problem: No source found for 'very similar' Ugaritic festivals, and the claim that Israel took over and 'transformed' agricultural festivals is a scholarly theory stated as fact. Leviticus 23 itself gives a historical reason only for Sukkot (23:43).
evidence: Leviticus 23:43 'in order that future generations may know that I made the Israelite people live in booths when I brought them out of the land of Egypt' (the only historical reason in the chapter). https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Leviticus.23.43?version=english
fix: Many scholars think these began as harvest festivals and were later tied to Israel's history. In Leviticus 23 only Sukkot is given a historical reason: the booths recall the wilderness (23:43); Passover is tied to the Exodus in Exodus 12, and Shavuot became the day of the giving of the Torah in rabbinic tradition.

current: The Priestly Laws — Julius Schnorr von Carolsfeld, 1860
problem: The file is a pen-and-wash drawing by Niccolò dell'Abbate (d. 1571). Commons calls it 'The Blasphemer' (Lev 24:13-23) but notes that the Louvre titles it 'The stoning of the prophet Jeremiah', so the scene is uncertain. It is not Schnorr and not 'The Priestly Laws'.
evidence: Commons File:Abbate The Blasphemer.jpg: 'The Blasphemer, as in Leviticus 24:13-23, by Niccolò dell'Abbate (1509 or 1512 – 1571); pen, brown ink… at the Musée du Louvre, Paris; according to the Louvre database, the title of this work is "The stoning of the prophet Jeremiah"'. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Abbate_The_Blasphemer.jpg
fix: A stoning (catalogued by the Louvre as The Stoning of the Prophet Jeremiah) — Niccolò dell'Abbate  [scene uncertain; consider replacing with a picture securely of Leviticus 24]

current: The practical consequence is that land in Israel can never be permanently sold — only leased until the next Jubilee, with the price calibrated to years remaining.
problem: True of farmland ('ancestral holdings'), but a house in a walled city that is not redeemed within a year passes to the buyer permanently and does not return in the Jubilee.
evidence: Leviticus 25:30 'the house in the walled city shall pass to the purchaser beyond reclaim throughout the ages; it shall not be released in the jubilee.' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Leviticus.25.29-30?version=english
fix: The practical consequence is that farmland can never be sold for good, only leased until the next Jubilee, with the price set by the years remaining (25:15–16); houses in walled cities are the exception (25:29–30).

current: Scholars debate whether the Jubilee was ever actually practiced, since it would require an entire country to simultaneously cease agricultural production for a full year every fifty years — an extraordinary economic disruption.
problem: The reason given for the scholarly doubt is the writer's own inference, not a sourced argument. The Talmud itself says the Jubilee lapsed when the tribes east of the Jordan were exiled.
evidence: Leviticus 25:11 'you shall not sow, neither shall you reap the aftergrowth' (the rule itself); Arakhin 32b: 'From the time that the tribe of Reuben and the tribe of Gad and half the tribe of Manasseh were exiled, the counting of Jubilee Years was nullified' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Arakhin.32b
fix: Scholars debate whether the Jubilee was ever carried out. The Talmud (Arakhin 32b) says the counting of Jubilee years stopped once the tribes of Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh were exiled.

current: ...complex halakhic workarounds called 'heter mechira' (selling the land to a non-Jew for the year) are used by many farmers while others — particularly in the religious-Zionist community — practice full Shemitah observance.
problem: The groups are reversed. The heter mechira is administered by the Chief Rabbinate and accepted in Modern Orthodox / religious-Zionist circles; the main opposition comes from Haredi authorities, who follow the Chazon Ish.
evidence: Wikipedia, 'Shmita': the heter mechira 'was later adopted by the Chief Rabbinate of Israel as a permanent edict, generating ongoing controversy between Zionist and Haredi leaders'; 'The heter mechira was accepted by Modern Orthodox Judaism… has met with opposition, particularly from Haredi poskim'. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shmita
fix: Many farmers use the 'heter mechira', a sale of the land to a non-Jew for the year, arranged by the Chief Rabbinate; many Haredi authorities reject it and look for other arrangements.

current: The Shemitah (sabbatical year) is one of the few Torah agricultural laws with direct archaeological evidence for ancient practice. Nehemiah 10:32 records the people of Jerusalem pledging to observe the seventh-year release of land; the Maccabean period includes references to food shortages during sabbatical years; and documents from the Dead Sea Scrolls community reflect sabbatical year observance.
problem: The examples are written sources, not archaeology. Nehemiah's pledge is by the returned community (not only Jerusalem) to forgo seventh-year produce and debts. The Dead Sea Scrolls claim was not verified here.
evidence: Nehemiah 10:32 'We will forgo [the produce of] the seventh year, and every outstanding debt.' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Nehemiah.10.32?version=english ; 1 Maccabees 6 (Brenton): 'their vessels being without victuals, (for that it was the seventh year…)' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/The_Book_of_Maccabees_I.6
fix: Unlike the Jubilee, the sabbatical year is mentioned as actually kept in later sources: in Nehemiah 10:32 the returned exiles pledge to forgo the produce of the seventh year and all debts, and 1 Maccabees 6 says a siege went badly for the Jews because 'it was the seventh year'.

current: The Year of Jubilee — Julius Schnorr von Carolsfeld, 1860
problem: The file is a photograph by Olve Utne of a Yemenite shofar made from kudu horn, not a Schnorr artwork. It fits the Jubilee shofar (25:9) only as a modern object photo; CC BY-SA 2.5 requires crediting Olve Utne.
evidence: Commons File:Jemenittisk sjofar av kuduhorn.jpg: 'A Temani (Yemeni Jewish) style shofar made from a horn of the greater kudu'; Artist 'Olve Utne'; 'Please credit this photo to Olve Utne'; CC BY-SA 2.5. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Jemenittisk_sjofar_av_kuduhorn.jpg
fix: A Yemenite shofar of kudu horn (photo) — Olve Utne

current: ...the curses escalate in seven waves, each preceded by 'and if after this you still do not listen to me.'
problem: There are five rounds (26:14, 18, 21, 23, 27), each worded somewhat differently; the number seven belongs to the refrain 'sevenfold for your sins'.
evidence: Leviticus 26:18 'if, for all that, you do not obey Me, I will go on to discipline you sevenfold'; 26:21 'if you remain hostile toward Me… sevenfold'; 26:23-24 '…I in turn will smite you sevenfold'; 26:27-28 'But if, despite this, you disobey Me… I… will discipline you sevenfold for your sins.' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Leviticus.26.27-28?version=english
fix: The curses rise in five rounds (26:14, 18, 21, 23, 27); each time Israel still refuses to listen, God warns of punishment 'sevenfold for your sins'.

current: Yet even at the bottom of this abyss, there is a turn: God promises that even in exile, if even one of them returns, God will remember the covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob — and the land — and will not utterly destroy them or break the covenant with them.
problem: 'If even one of them returns' is not in the text. The text speaks of the people confessing and their heart humbling (26:40-41), names the patriarchs in reverse order (Jacob, Isaac, Abraham), and the promise not to destroy them (26:44) is stated without condition.
evidence: Leviticus 26:40-42 'they shall confess their iniquity… then at last shall their obdurate heart humble itself… Then will I remember My covenant with Jacob; I will remember also My covenant with Isaac, and also My covenant with Abraham'; 26:44 'Yet, even then, when they are in the land of their enemies, I will not reject them or spurn them so as to destroy them.' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Leviticus.26.40-42?version=english
fix: Yet even at the bottom there is a turn: when the exiles confess and their hearts are humbled, God will remember the covenant with Jacob, Isaac and Abraham, and the land (26:40–42); and even in the land of their enemies God will not reject them or break the covenant with them (26:44).

current: Jewish law specifies that both are to be read in a single Torah reading without interruption... The curses are written in the second person singular ('you' — meaning Israel as an individual), while the Deuteronomy curses shift to plural and are generally considered more severe.
problem: Reversed. The Talmud says the Leviticus curses are in the plural, spoken by Moses from God's mouth and therefore more severe, so they may not be split between readers; the Deuteronomy curses are in the singular, and Abaye allows them to be split. Neither text says both are read together in one reading.
evidence: Megillah 31b (Abaye): 'They taught this only with regard to the curses that are recorded in Leviticus, but with regard to the curses that are recorded in Deuteronomy, one may interrupt them… These curses in Leviticus are stated in the plural, and Moses pronounced them from the mouth of the Almighty. As such, they are more severe. However, these curses in Deuteronomy are stated in the singular, and Moses said them on his own… They are therefore less harsh and may be interrupted.' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Megillah.31b
fix: The curses are read without a break, as a single aliyah (Mishnah Megillah 3:6). The Talmud (Megillah 31b) notes that the curses here are in the plural and were spoken by Moses from God's mouth, so they are treated as the more severe; those in Deuteronomy are in the singular.

current: ...and the reader traditionally chants them in a very low voice — some congregations have a tradition of the Torah reader being unpaid for this section, since 'no one wants the job.'
problem: No source found for an 'unpaid reader' custom; the recorded custom is the reverse: people avoided being called up for the curses, and the Maharil held that only the sexton hired for it should go up. The low-voice custom was not verified here.
evidence: Magen Avraham on Orach Chayim 428:8: 'Maharil objected to one who went up for the rebuke—specifically, only the sexton hired for this has no issue.' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Magen_Avraham.428.8
fix: Because people were reluctant to be called up for the curses, some communities had the hired sexton take this aliyah (Magen Avraham on Orach Chayim 428, citing the Maharil).

current: Both Tochachot have been read by generations of Jews as predictions of the actual catastrophes that befell the Jewish people: the Assyrian exile, the Babylonian exile, the Roman conquest, and the Holocaust.
problem: Vague 'generations of Jews' with no source. The classic source, Nachmanides, ties the Leviticus curses specifically to the First Temple and the Babylonian exile.
evidence: Ramban on Leviticus 26:16: 'Know and understand that these oaths [stated in this section] allude to the first exile [i.e., the Babylonian exile following the destruction of the First Temple]' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Ramban_on_Leviticus.26.16
fix: Nachmanides (on 26:16) reads the curses here as pointing to the destruction of the First Temple and the Babylonian exile; later readers have also seen in them the disasters of later Jewish history.

current: The Midrash (Sifra on Lev. 26:44) lists four times God promises not to reject Israel in exile, corresponding to the four empires of oppression, and concludes: 'if not for these four phrases, Israel could not survive among the nations.'
problem: The Sifra does tie the phrases of 26:44 to Vespasian (Rome), Greece, Haman and the Chaldeans, plus Gog and Magog, but the quoted conclusion is not in it. The nearest line says that if not for the Torah scroll left to them, they would be no different from the nations.

"to destroy them": in the days of Haman. "to break My covenant with them": in the days of the Kasdim. "for I am the L–rd their G-d": in the days of Gog and Magog' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Sifra,_Bechukotai,_Chapter_8 ; similar baraita in Megillah 11a https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Megillah.11a

current: Hittite suzerainty treaties from the second millennium BCE uniformly end with a list of divine witnesses and curses on the vassal who violates the treaty terms — including military defeat, agricultural failure, exile, and cannibalism during siege. ... The Torah uses exactly the same treaty-curse format to describe the Israel-God covenant, framing the relationship as a formal suzerainty agreement.
problem: 'Uniformly' and the specific list (exile, cannibalism in siege) are not supported for Hittite treaties; the siege-cannibalism curses are known from the Neo-Assyrian treaties of Esarhaddon, which scholars compare mainly with Deuteronomy 28. 'Exactly the same format' overstates; sources stress Deuteronomy is not simply a treaty.
evidence: Wikipedia, 'Book of Deuteronomy': 'Other scholars have compared the structure of Deuteronomy with Hittite treaties… But it is clear that Deuteronomy is not in itself simply the text of a treaty'; Weinfeld noted 'substantive affinities between the blessings and curses that appear in the book and the vassal treaties of Esarhaddon'. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Book_of_Deuteronomy ; Wikipedia 'Ki Tavo': 'Plaut reported general scholarly agreement that the vassal treaties of the Assyrian King Esarhaddon influenced these curses.' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ki_Tavo
fix: Treaties in the ancient Near East often ended with blessings and curses called down by the gods named as witnesses. Scholars compare the curses in Leviticus 26 and especially Deuteronomy 28 with the vassal treaties of the Assyrian king Esarhaddon (672 BCE), and many see the covenant here as shaped on the treaty model.
